The formulation of monetary policy by Eugenio Domingo Solans Member of the Governing Council and the Executive Committee of the European Central Bank. Intervention in the XXVI Days of the Financial Markets. Sevilla, 3 June 1999. I think it is best to spend time available to comment on some specific aspects of the ECB's monetary policy with the intention of helping them to be better understood by the public and by the markets and, at least, not to cause them to make mistakes. This means that although the priority objective of the Eurosystem is price stability or, if preferred, internal stability, Article 105 of the Treaty on European Union introduces a secondary objective by establishing that "without prejudice to this objective (Statility), the European System of Central Banks (SEC) will support the general economic policies of the Community with a view to contributing to the Community's objectives", including those contained in Article 2 of the Treaty - "a sustainable and non-inflationary growth which respects the environment" and "a high level of employment and social protection". My personal interpretation of this SEBC's secondary objective is part of the agreement that, in the medium term, the best contribution that the Eurosystem can make in favour of sustained growth, job creation and social protection is precisely creating a stable environment. Stability is socially just and inflation is spread to society. On the other hand, there is no better heat for growth of economic growth than price stability, there is nothing less than inflation. I said "the best contribution," but I think it is not possible. In other words, the Eurosystem can neither ignore its secondary objective nor sustain its implementation with its own "first-time" purpose with only "rememovableness." In this regard, it should be accepted that, in the short term, the possibility of a compromise between the degree of stability and economic growth, and that I say a compromise between "the degree of stability" and growth and not a commitment between "the stability" to drought and growth. In technical terms, it should be admitted that monetary policy can in the short term affect both prices (stabilities) and quantities (creating), which do not occur in the long term in which monetary policy alone affects prices. Note that in the previous formulation there are used expressions as "the ability to grow", "can affect", which relate to affirmation. In terms of economic growth and in a short term, it may not be the same as inflation level of, for example, 0.5% that one of us says, 1.5%, especially if, in order to achieve or maintain the first one, there is a very restrictive monetary policy. Of course, the degree of restriction of monetary policy required to obtain a certain level of stability varies in many circumstances, such as the cyclical position of the economy or the existence of effects on the offer. Similarly, at the time of making a decision on monetary policy, which is like to be sure at the time of deciding to change the degree of stability that exists, it is as difficult as relevant: neither too soon nor too late, with the aim of meeting the objective of stability without negatively affecting growth expectations. In conclusion, and in the short term, it is not true how much more stability and how much it is always preferable. Any increase in prices is sufficiently small or short to avoid distortions in the price mechanism (in relation to the Austrian school approach) or sufficiently small or short to not require the application of a general indication process (in relation to the classical and neoclastic aspects of monetary neutrality) is compatible with the concept of stability. The ECB understands that this is the case when the annual increase in the Harmonised Price Index to the Consumer (HICP) for the whole of the euro remains below 2% in a medium term. Firstly, the ECB has a quantitative definition of "under 2%" and not an annual objective, i.e. it is a permanent commitment. In contrast, for example, the Bank of England, which receives annual inflation targets (currently, 2.5%), has a quantitative definition of stability established by itself which, as such, is not revisable annually. However, it should be admitted that, from the perspective of a monetary policy strategy based on inflation, there is no real difference between setting up an inflation objective or a quantitative definition of inflation (currently, 2%), which is defined by many differentials which are based on a general rate of inflation which is based on the difference between the rate of 2% or 2%. THE STRATEGY The first thing I would like to say about the ECB's monetary policy is precisely this, which is a strategy and not a mix of policies which are used by the BCN. In the final product you need a label, a brand, rather than a purely descriptive name of "monetary policy strategy aimed at stability". Our strength is not marketing. In this context, the M3 increase of 41/2% is a reference and not a target and therefore the claim that no one should expect a mechanical reaction from the monetary policy before possible deviations seems to be justified. It is also considered that the existence of a second pillar which is designed to complement the traditional monetary strategy, consisting of the assessment of future developments in prices and risks for the euro area in terms of a range of indicators of inflation. I believe that the degree of specification of the two pillars of the ECB's monetary policy strategy, complemented by its six, is sufficient to allow markets to understand the decision-making of the ECB which is important for the effectiveness of the measure adopted. It provides a framework or a general environment mainly aimed at stability and, without prejudice to it, to support general economic policies by creating conditions conducive to economic growth, but all of this in a "passive" way, before, such as the air that breathes, not as an oxygen ball. In the traditional dilemma between rules and discretionaryness, the ECB is much more likely to extend the scope of economic debt and, therefore, to improve conditions for sustained economic growth. A third feature of the ECB's monetary policy formulation is the lack of autonomy, in order that decisions which are taken are not a mechanical response to changes in the value of variables. I am aware that the inability to discriminate regionally is a general feature of any monetary policy, but it must be agreed that the economic, financial, political and institutional nature of the euro area makes this point particularly sensitive. The effects of monetary policy in each country or region can be different, depending on the various relevant factors. One of them is the different levels of inflation from each country or region, which will involve different types of real and market intervention, which can cause local proc­cal effects. However, it is reasonable to understand that the ECB is obliged to adopt a global perspective throughout the area when it formulates monetary policy and does not make the mistake of interpreting the ECB's decisions from a national perspective.
